commonly stored in CPDA. Individuals with the Co(b) allele are at high risk for adverse reactions during this procedure, rare examples of which include TRALI ("trolley") and TACO. The Curry-Howard correspondence describes the direct relationship between computer programs and these constructs, which can be arranged using Fitch notation. One spurious early work in this author's namesake Appendix includes the stories of famous Roman heroes narrated by a gnat. The Spectre exploit observed differences in this variable to detect successful instances of speculative execution. Hedda Sterne was the only female member of a photograph featuring 18 artists of this movement. This author wrote a story for children about a firework that bursts into tears and fails to ignite, "The Remarkable Rocket." In C++, buffers for files and these entities are the two standard derived classes of streambuf. In C, placeholders featuring percent signs format these entities. A virtuoso of this instrument wrote a set of Opus 73 etudes called the High School of [playing this instrument] as well as short showpieces for it like Spinnlied and Elfentanz. A variant of this experiment used a puppy instead of people so subjects wouldn't suspect it of faking. The ratio of two values of this quantity equals the exponential of delta H over R times the difference of the reciprocals of temperatures. This musician's son is the current tenor saxophonist of the Blue Note 7, and their wife played both piano and harp in her album Journey in Satchidananda. This character exclaims, "There it is! The door you love to slam in my face," in the deleted song "Life's Too Short." Anna of Arendelle [accept Princess or Queen Anna of Arendelle]

A 1932 photograph taken in this city depicts a man mid-leap over a large puddle. The protagonist of this novel uses a coracle made of wood and goat-skin to board a schooner, which they set adrift before killing the coxswain ("COX-en") Israel Hands. Treasure Island [or Treasure Island or the Mutiny of the Hispaniola; accept The Sea Cook: A Story for Boys]

Every six years, this country hosts a music competition that was won in 2021 by Bruce Liu. The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory was built in a mine at a large example of these sites, which may be identified by their breccia ("BREK-i-a") lenses. Susan Haack is a scholar of a thinker from this movement, and rejects the author of Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature's claim of belonging to its "neo-" branch. Romania [or Socialist Republic of Romania; accept Romanian People’s Republic]

Grypania, one of these organisms, is found in the oldest identifiable eukaryotic fossil. These organisms include chlorophytes and charophytes. algae [accept red algae or green algae; accept algal bloom; accept cyanobacteria until “events”, and reject after]

This philosopher interpreted propositions concerning contingent future events using the example of a sea battle that will happen tomorrow. Description acceptable. Every October 18th, a member of this family does the same interview with Vanity Fair and brings on its matriarch at its end. O’Connell [or any answer designating the family of Billie Eilish; accept Baird; accept Billie Eilish Pirate Baird O’Connell; accept Finneas Baird O’Connell]

In a novella by this author, a group of characters bizarrely declare that they will "marry unsound and unhealthy" mates in order "to eradicate evil heredity." In this novel, a character calls a movie accompanied by a scent organ "base" and "ignoble." A "Coalition" of evangelical churches named for this concept is led by D. A. Carson and Tim Keller. One ruler of this empire abandoned his wine-filled camp to allow the Massagetae to inebriate themselves before his forces slaughtered them. The third stanza of George Seferis' poem "Mythistorema" was recited at the beginning of one of these events. A multinucleate cell in this organ is formed by the endogenous retrovirus element syncytin and helps limit the extravasation of white blood cells. This poet described a figure being "unmoved" by pausing chariots and kneeling emperors at her mat. This poet may not have ever sent three letters addressed to an unnamed "Master." screaming [accept Echo of a Scream; accept the Screaming Popes; accept The Scream]

The Dong-A ("dong-ah") Ilbo newspaper removed one of these objects from a picture after Son Kee-Chung won the marathon at the 1936 Olympics. A civil war in this country took a turn after one side, led by British naval officer George Sartorius, landed at Mindelo. Indigenous people on this island joined enslaved Wolof people in a Christmas day rebellion. An invading force in this island was resisted by the Ciguayos by the Bay of Arrows. In one of their Four Dissertations this thinker discussed how "taste" is developed. The Resurrection was questioned by this thinker in the section "On Miracles." Two characters in this novel duel with spears but swing them like swords to avoid killing one another. The Helicon sank underground to prevent some Maenads from performing this action. The nymph Salmacis attacked Hermaphroditus while he was taking this action. washing [or ablution; accept answers like bathing or cleaning by water; prompt on cleansing or cleaning or purifying by asking “How exactly?”; prompt on swimming and equivalents] (The Maenads who killed Orpheus tried to wash the blood off in the Helicon, but failed.)

In a novel by this author, the title character and their dog Tiger sneak onto the ship Grampus. The narrator is suffocated by the smell of "heated iron" in a story by this author. In this country, the Nandi leader Koitalel Samoei attempted to stop a railroad whose construction was also slowed by attacks from the Tsavo Maneaters. Argentina national football team [accept Argentine or Argentinian national football team; accept La Albiceleste before mention; accept soccer in place of football]

A process where this technique is performed in reverse utilizes excess silver nitrate. It isn't Iran, but a kingdom sharing its name with this modern country was ruled by the Arsacid Dynasty. Mark-Anthony Turnage and Kaija Saariaho contributed to a 2005 project by Simon Rattle intended to complement this piece. The Haymarket Theatre premiered a play by this author in which despite Mrs. Cheveley's blackmail, Lady Chiltern forgives her husband for not being "An Ideal Husband." In a play by this author, the title woman goes to Lord (*) Darlington's apartment as a lover is discovered by her fan. Lady Bracknell agrees to Gwendolyn's marriage to Jack Worthing, the long-lost brother of Algernon Moncrieff in this author's The Importance of Being Earnest. For 10 points, name this Irish author tried and imprisoned for homosexuality.

Sudbury, Ontario is a major nickel mining center due to one of these features filling with magma. Frederic Daniel Johnson died on the way to inaugurate a dam that flooded one of these features named Manicouagan, the "Eye of Quebec." The gold of the Witwatersrand is exposed because crustal rebound within one of these features created the Vredefort Dome. A circular ring of sinkholes helped geologists identify one of these features named (*) Chicxulub, which supported Walter and Luis Alvarez's theories about the K-Pg boundary and the extinction of the dinosaurs. For 10 points, name these features formed by the impacts of asteroids and meteorites.

Eryx was founded when Aphrodite took Butes ("beauties") as her lover after saving him from these figures. Palinurus's death is discovered near these figures' land. Orpheus wins a music contest against these figures in the Argonautica by being louder than them. These figures name the order of sea cows because medieval bestiaries reimagined them as (*) sexually tempting mermaids. These figures had to throw themselves off a cliff if anyone passed them alive, so the last two of them died after Odysseus's sailors bound him to the mast and plugged their own ears with beeswax. For 10 points, name these part-bird women whose song lured men to wreck their ships, lending their name to loud devices on police cars.

An "error-prone" version of this technique is used to get a mutant library. Off-target hits can be reduced with this technique's "touchdown" variety, which requires a "hot start." Fluorescent dyes allow this technique to be made "real-time," or "quantitative." In this technique, primers bind to the starts of desired DNA strands and have dNTPs added to them by heat-resistant (*) Taq polymerase. This technique's "reverse transcriptase" type handles RNA. This technique uses a thermal cycler to achieve denaturation, annealing, and extension stages to amplify a DNA sample in a chain reaction. For 10 points, name this technique that is used in the most precise COVID tests.

A blue variant of this plant that contains hallucinogenic aporphine was the first thing to emerge from the primeval ocean Nun. Nefertem is associated with this plant, which with papyrus and palm are the inspirations for Egyptian columns' capitals. Lakshmi often holds this plant while sitting in a position with feet over her thighs named for it, the (*) padmasana. Due to its ultrahydrophobicity, thrones in the shape of this plant symbolize purity in Indian religions. Men who eat a flower of this name lose all desire except to continue eating it in the Odyssey. For 10 points, the Buddha compares himself to and sits atop what flower that grows in muddy ponds?

This city's Opzoomer Street names a type of community-organized urban renewal movement. The Lijnbaan shopping street in this city was the first planned pedestrian street in Europe. Ossip Zadkine's sculpture The Destroyed City commemorates this city's World War II bombing. Dubbed "The Swan" for its asymmetrical pylon, this city's Erasmus Bridge crosses the New Meuse River. This is the largest city protected by the Delta Works. Due to its (*) Europoort, this city in the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt Delta is the largest seaport in Europe. For 10 points, name this city that forms a metropolitan area with The Hague and is the second largest city in the Netherlands.

Moderator note: Read the bass sequence slowly. Note to players: The answer to this question is a recurring musical theme. You may name the theme if it has a colloquial name, like "the lick," or describe the theme uniquely by naming the piece it originally featured in, and, if necessary, the context within the piece. Handel's G major chaconnes with 21 and 62 variations on this theme, HWV 435 and 442, likely inspired its most famous use. 14 canons on this theme, rediscovered on an autograph score, use its G-major bass "G, F-sharp 6, E sharp-6, D, B 6, C 6, D, G." Johann Forkel suggested that folk songs including "Cabbage and turnips have driven me away" were paired with this theme in a (*) "quodlibet" as a joke. A six-voice canon on this theme is shown in the one confirmed portrait of J. S. Bach. Wanda Landowska described a minor-key variation of this theme as a "black pearl." For 10 points, 30 keyboard variations on what theme were written for Count Keyserling's insomnia by J. S. Bach?

the ground bass of the Goldberg Variations [accept any answer that says Goldberg in it; prompt on any answer that uses the note string in the question beginning “G F-sharp E D” etc. by asking “what piece is that most famously used in?”]

In the language of these people, orenda refers to the spiritual power within a thing. Catherine Tekakwitha, one of these people, was canonized after miracles followed her death at Kahnawake. Cornplanter supported the replacement of Christianity with a religion of these people, Gaiwiio, that combines animist and Quaker beliefs in a "Good Word" and was founded by Handsome Lake. The white pine tree, or Tree of (*) Peace, represents the story of these people's origin codified in their Great Law of Peace. For 10 points, the Longhouse Religion is practiced by what Native American confederacy of upstate New York?
Haudenosaunee [accept Iroquois; accept Iroquoian; antiprompt on Mohawk, Seneca, Onondaga, Oneida, Cayuga, or Tuscarora with “what broader polity are they a part of?”]

This opera's overture begins with a "D C-sharp D C-sharp D" trill-like motif in the strings. In this opera, a boy escapes out of a window into Antonio's flowerpots after singing "Voi che sapete." Lorenzo da Ponte cleaned this opera's libretto to avoid the political ban on Pierre Beaumarchais's play. In this opera, a mezzo-soprano playing a lovesick teenage boy sings "Non so piu cosa son" and is told off for flirting in "Non piu andrai"; that boy is (*) Cherubino. This opera's title character helps his wife, Susanna, avoid the "right of the first night" being carried out by Duke Almaviva. For 10 points, name this opera named for the barber of Seville, written by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

A politician dubbed "the Liberator," who represented this city and names its main street, created the Lichfield House Compact with the Whigs. This city's Mansion House was home to the First and Second Dails ("doyles"). Lord Cavendish and Thomas Burke were murdered in this city's Phoenix Park, which forged letters pinned on Charles Parnell. This city's General (*) Post Office was the hub of a rebellion led by Patrick Pearse and the IRB whose defeat led to greater Sinn Fein sentiment. The Home Rule movement sought this city as a center for a regional parliament. For 10 points, name this city where the Easter Rising occurred, the capital of Ireland.

The substitution "u = [this function] of one-half x" simplifies many trigonometric integrals. The integral of this function is the natural logarithm of the secant function, while the derivative of its inverse is "1 over 1 plus x squared." The Pythagorean identity states that this function squared, plus 1, equals (*) secant squared. On a unit circle, this function of an angle is the slope of the line that forms that angle, as this function equals sine over cosine. For 10 points, name this function that equals the opposite side length over the adjacent side length for an angle in a right triangle, which shares its name with a line that just touches a curve at a point.
tangent [do not accept or prompt on “arctangent” or “inverse tangent”]

A chromatic octave run from C to G-sharp, then a first inversion A minor chord, opens this composer's "Little Red Riding Hood and the Wolf," one of his Etudes-Tableaux ("eh-TOOD tab-LOH"). This composer also wrote Morceaux de fantaisie ("MOR-soo day FON-tay-see"), which includes a piano piece notated on four staves, the Prelude in C-sharp minor. One piano concerto by this composer, in C minor, begins with quiet (*) bell-like chords alternating with a low F and was written after recovery from depression. This composer also wrote a set of piano variations on a theme from Paganini's 24th Caprice. For 10 points, name this Russian composer known for his massive hands who wrote Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini.

Tyrian purple consists of two atoms of this element attached to indigo. The Wohl-Ziegler reaction uses NBS as a stable source of this element's radical. It's not phosphorous, but organic derivatives of this element are the most common flame retardants. This element is the heavier of the two with an M+2 peak in mass spectroscopy due to nearly equal amounts of its 79 and 81 isotopes. (*) Grignard reagents are defined by magnesium and this element. This element is the second-heaviest diatomic element, and it and mercury are the only elements that are liquid at standard conditions. For 10 points, name this element, between chlorine and iodine in the halogens, with the symbol Br.

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia results from a cancer of these cells. These cells are named for their discovery in the avian bursa of Fabricius. The "regulatory" type of these cells produce IL-10. These cells are depleted with the monoclonal antibody rituximab, which attacks their CD20 receptors. CD27 marks the "memory" type of these cells, which can circulate in the blood for decades. These cells in the (*) adaptive immune system differentiate into plasma cells after internalizing antigens, which are the main cells that secrete antibodies. For 10 points, name these lymphocytes that do not mature in the thymus, unlike NK cells and T cells, and instead in the bone marrow.

An autoimmune disease of this molecule's receptors was the first approved indication of the first anti-FcRn drug; that disease is myasthenia gravis. Receptors for this molecule are classified by sensitivity to muscarine and nicotine. This molecule's esterase, which degrades it, is inhibited by sarin and other nerve agents. This molecule, norepinephrine, and (*) epinephrine are the main neurotransmitters of the autonomic nervous system. This molecule transmits signals from presynaptic nerves at neuromuscular junctions to stimulate muscle contraction. For 10 points, name this molecule, a derivative of choline ("KOH-leen").

Immediately north of this lake is the historic depot of Norway House, part of the York Factory Express. A major lake immediately west of this lake has the same name as it with the suffix "-osis." This lake is the largest remnant of Lake Agassiz. This lake's largest outflow is the Nelson River. Lake of the Woods empties into this lake through a river of the same name. The (*) Canadian prairies drain into this lake through the Saskatchewan River. The Assiniboine River joins the Red River of the North before their combined waters empty into this lake. For 10 points, name this largest lake in Manitoba, which shares its name with the province's capital.

According to legend, when one ruler of this polity had to kiss the king's foot, he raised the foot to his mouth, knocking him over. Queen Emma, wife to Ethelred the Unready and Cnut, hailed from this polity. The first leader of this polity was given it by Charles the Simple and had the title "jarl" ("yarl") and Latin name (*) Rollo. This polity's initial capitals were Caen and Rouen, the latter being changed to Bayeux by a duke who claimed that a shipwrecked Edward the Confessor had promised him his crown. The Vikings, or "Northmen," name, for 10 points, what region of northern France from which William the Conqueror invaded England?

This regime's warriors included Yoichi, who shot a fan off an enemy warship from horseback, and Kumagai, who tearfully killed his enemy's boy commander, as told in Tales of the Heike. This regime's eponymous capital contains a monumental bronze Buddha. This regime's founder forced his brother to commit suicide after leading his army to victory at Dan-no-ura. This regime, run by regents of the Hojo clan, ended with the Kenmu Restoration in (*) 1333. Two Mongol invasions were repelled by the kamikaze winds under this regime. For 10 points, the Genpei War against the Taira ended when Minamoto no Yoritomo founded what first shogunate of Japan, before the Ashikaga?

An artist in this city magically finds a bag of gold behind a portrait of a moneylender before giving up his genius for success. That story, "The Portrait," was in Arabesques before being republished in a collection titled "[this city] Tales." A man follows a beautiful woman on this place's central street before killing himself with opium because she is a prostitute. Until finding a certain "important personage," the ghost of (*) Akaky Akakievich steals overcoats in this city. After finding it in his wife's bread, Ivan Yakovlevich throws "the nose" into this city's Neva River. For 10 points, many of Nikolai Gogol's stories occur in what coastal former capital of Russia?
St. Petersburg [or Petrograd] (The unnamed stories are “Nevsky Prospekt,” “The Overcoat,” and “The Nose.”)

A red crescent of sand called the Dahna stretches south from this region's Nufud. This region's Dhofar Mountains stretch into its Hadhramaut region. The Hajar Mountains, this region's highest, stretch into its northeastern point at Musandam. This region's heaviest rainfall is in its Sarawat Mountains, which contain subranges named Asir and (*) Hejaz. This region is the largest peninsula in the world. This peninsula's Nejd central plateau lies north of the Rub' al-Khali, a sandy part of its namesake desert that connects to the Sahara. For 10 points, name this peninsula between the Persian Gulf and Red Sea whose largest country is ruled by the House of Saud.

Description acceptable. The original statement of Bell's theorem concerns two particles, each in this system. This system can be represented with a 3D diagram where antipodal points are orthogonal vectors, the Bloch sphere. This system can be described in bra-ket notation as alpha ket 0 plus beta ket 1, where alpha squared and beta squared are the probabilities of being in ket 0 or ket 1 once superposition is broken. The (*) Stern-Gerlach experiment showed that electron angular momentum is an example of this system. For 10 points, name this two-state quantum system, the basic unit of quantum information and the analogue to the bit in quantum computing.

qubit [accept quantum bit before “bit” and prompt afterwards; accept descriptions of a two-state quantum system before mention; accept singlet in first sentence; prompt on quantum system by asking “with how many states?”; do not accept or prompt on “bit”]

This colony's indigenous slaves were called "blacks of the land" to distinguish them from Africans. This colony was initially split into 15 private "captaincies" for settlement. This colony's expansion into the sertao was largely due to the Bandeirantes, Paulistas who raided its Tupi people for slaves. This colony was the world's largest exporter of sugarcane by the 17th century, and its name derives from the (*) dyewood that was its first main export. This colony was first claimed by Pedro Alvares Cabral in 1500 and initially lay east of the Treaty of Tordesillas line. For 10 points, name this colony whose first capital, Salvador, was replaced by Rio de Janeiro.

It's not the substrate, but drugs are often made to be analogs of this configuration in order to inhibit enzymes that stabilize it. In an endothermic reaction, this configuration looks more like the products than the reactants by Hammond's postulate. The Eyring equation modifies the Arrhenius equation by incorporating theories about this configuration. This configuration is drawn in square brackets with a superscript (*) double dagger. States similar to this one can be called the "activated complex," and the difference between reactant energy and this state's energy is the activation energy. For 10 points, name this state, the short-lived, highest-energy step of a reaction.

When asked about his neighbors, this play's protagonist says, "I cannot judge another. I have no tongue for it." In response to his wife's suspicions, that character exclaims, "your justice would freeze beer!" In this play, a character declares that "God is dead" during a scene of chaos induced by an invisible yellow bird. The wife of this play's protagonist says that he has "found his goodness" by its end; earlier, he shouts "I have given you my soul; leave me my (*) name!" when refusing to sign a false confession. Elizabeth ultimately forgives John Proctor for his affair with Abigail Williams in, for 10 points, what Arthur Miller play that allegorizes McCarthyism with the Salem Witch Trials?

Artists transitioning away from painting on this material invented "ledger art." American Horse and other artists named each year for its most important event and drew pictographs on this material that depicted key events of the year in the "Winter Count" tradition. Painted robes of this material were often also decorated with porcupine quills. This material was the main one used west of the (*) Mississippi for coats and moccasins, and it was the primary component of a tipi cover. For 10 points, name this material whose supply was decimated by hunters, the skin of the largest animal on the Great Plains.
bison hide [accept skin or fur in place of “hide”; accept buffalo in place of bison; prompt on partial answers by asking either “of what animal?” or “what part of it?”]

These people's lands were subject to "the Ruin," during which they led an autonomous state after the Truce of Andrusovo. These people were subject to mass executions in 1919 after declaring independent states around the Kuban and Don Rivers. The Khanate of Sibir was overthrown by one of these people, Yermak. These people won the (*) Khmelnytsky Uprising against Poland-Lithuania. The Zaporozhian hetman of these people, Ivan Mazepa, defected to Sweden during the Great Northern War. A revolt of these people against Catherine the Great was led by Yemelyan Pugachev. For 10 points, name these people of the Russian and Ukrainian steppes famous for their mounted cavalry.

The nine point center is the midpoint between the point where these lines intersect and the orthocenter. Multiplying the side lengths of a triangle and dividing by four times its area gives a length defined by the point where these lines intersect, denoted capital R. These lines can be constructed by drawing circles of equal radius from two points and (*) connecting their intersections. These lines in a triangle intersect at the circumcenter, which is equidistant from all three vertices. These lines are the locuses of points equidistant from two given points. For 10 points, name these lines defined by intersecting the midpoint of a line segment at a right angle.
perpendicular bisector [do not accept or prompt on partial answer]

Quinctilius Varus, who died at the Teutoburg Forest, crushed a 4 BC revolt in the immediate predecessor of this province against the ethnarch Archelaus. Caesarea Maritima first became a provincial capital at this province's creation, which also saw Rome annex the regions of Edom and Samaria. Prior to Nero's deposition, Vespasian was fighting a war in this province, whose final siege was completed by Titus and commemorated on his (*) "arch." The last holdouts of that revolt in this province, the Zealots, were described by Josephus as killing each other to avoid capture as the Romans retook Masada. For 10 points, name this Roman province whose King Herod the Great was given the title "King of the Jews."

Parallel stories of a World War II veteran with PTSD and heroes traveling in the "Fourth World" make up one novel from this country, Confessions by Leslie Marmon Silko. One author from this country combined legend, history, and memoir in The Way to Rainy Mountain and started a "renaissance" with House Made of Dawn; that author is N. Scott Momaday. (*) Love Medicine was the debut novel by an author from this country who also wrote a novel where Thomas Wazhashk blocks the "termination" of Turtle Mountain Reservation, The Night Watchman. For 10 points, name this country where Louise Erdrich won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize awarded by Columbia University.
United States of America [accept US or USA; prompt on America]

The 1926 song "Chuck Out the Men" advocates expelling men from this location. The Kroll Opera House opposite this location replaced it for 12 years. Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic from this location during the November Revolution. In 1995, Jeanne-Claude and Cristo wrapped this location in canvas after 24 years of lobbying. Norman Foster's glass dome was added to this building in 1999. Marinus van der Lubbe set a (*) fire in this building that Paul von Hindenburg responded to with a "decree" suspending civil liberties that allowed the Nazi Party to round up political opponents. For 10 points, name this building that houses the Bundestag, Germany's Parliament.
Reichstag [prompt on German Parliament Building or other descriptions of a central governmental building of Germany]

This god, Pontus, and the hills were formed by their mother's parthenogenesis. This god was the father of Brontes, Steropes, and Arges, as well as the Hecatonchires, while his blood became the Meliae, Giants, and Furies. The Theogony states that Aphrodite was born from this god's genitals after he hid his children within their mother (*) Gaia, leading her to give one of her sons a flint or adamantine sickle to take revenge. This god's children, the Titans, succeeded him in rule after his castration by his son Kronos. For 10 points, name this Greek god of the sky who names the seventh planet from the sun.

Robert W. Wilson, co-discoverer of the CMBR, used this compound's 2.6 mm emission line and hydrogen gas's 21 cm line to make the first images of molecular clouds. The formation of ground-level ozone usually begins with this compound's reaction with hydroxyl radicals. The water-gas shift reaction forms hydrogen gas and CO2 from this compound and water. This compound is isoelectronic with cyanide and has one resonance structure containing a (*) coordinate covalent bond within a triple bond from carbon to oxygen. For 10 points, name this odorless gas that forms from incomplete combustion, which kills by displacing oxygen on hemoglobin and has chemical symbol CO.

Around half of all surviving Hellenistic works in this medium are from Delos. This medium's "vermiculatum," or "worm-like," style was used for faces and central panels during Roman times. A work in this medium found at the House of the Faun in Pompeii shows the victory of Alexander the Great at Issus. The Basilica of San Vitale's depictions of Theodora and Justinian in this medium had (*) tesserae infused with gold leaf, typical of Byzantine works in this medium. Upper-class Roman houses had floors decorated in this medium. For 10 points, name this medium in which an image is made of irregular fragments of stone or glass.

While working for this scientist, Julius Richard Petri invented the Petri dish by improving an agar-based device this scientist invented. This scientist incorrectly claimed that a protein now the subject of the Mantoux diagnostic test, tuberculin, actually cured tuberculosis. A causative agent must be absent from healthy individuals and cause disease when given to them, according to some of this scientist's namesake (*) postulates. Germany's disease control agency is named for this scientist, who won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1905 for discovering the tuberculosis bacteria. For 10 points, name this scientist and rival of Louis Pasteur, often called the "father of microbiology."

In this author's first novel, Arthur impregnates Hetty Sorrel, who is sentenced to death for child murder for abandoning her baby. In this author's last novel, the title character saves Mirah and Gwendolyn from suicide and marries Mirah upon learning his Jewish ancestry, following her brother Mordecai to "the East" to support Zionism. This author of Adam Bede and (*) Daniel Deronda also created the unsuccessful doctor Tertius Lydgate and an intellectual writing the out-of-date The Key to All Mythologies, Edward Casaubon, who rejects his wife Dorothea Brooke's assistance. For 10 points, name this pseudonymous female author of Middlemarch.

The Livingstone Lab suggests that this painting's appearance is affected by peripheral vision favoring lower spatial frequencies. Nude versions of this painting are titled for a "Lady Vanna," and Salai or Francesco Melzi most likely painted its Prado version. The Ponte Buriano is depicted above a person's shoulder in this painting's imaginary landscape, which is painted with prominent aerial perspective and (*) sfumato. Scans of this painting agree with Vasari that it once had eyebrows. Francis I brought this painting to France after its artist's death, and it is now the most-visited work at the Louvre. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci portrait of a lady with an elusive smile.
Mona Lisa [accept La Gioconda] (The effect in the first line is the elusiveness of the smile; she seems more smiling when you look more indirectly at the painting)

The Presevo ("PREH-sheh-voh") insurgency began after this war. The rejection of the Rambouillet ("rahn-boo-YEH") Agreement in this war resulted in Wesley Clark beginning Operation Allied Force, leading to the Kumanovo Agreement. One side blamed bad CIA maps for their bombing of a Chinese embassy in this war. The question of sending ground troops to this war was disagreed upon between (*) Tony Blair and Bill Clinton. In this war, NATO air raids against Belgrade, the center of Slobodan Milosevic's government, were prompted by claims of ethnic cleansing of Albanians. For 10 points, name this 1998-99 war within the Yugoslav Wars, named for what is now the youngest country in Europe.

The only binomial coefficient "n choose k," with k greater than 2, that is one of these numbers is 50 choose 3. Legendre proved that all natural numbers not equal to "4 to the a, times the quantity 8b plus 7" are the sum of three of these numbers; Lagrange then showed that all natural numbers are the sum of four of them. Fermat proved that an odd prime is the sum of two of these numbers if and only if it is 1 mod 4. The sum of the first n (*) odd numbers is the nth one of these numbers. These numbers are the only ones with an odd number of factors. These numbers form the main diagonal on the multiplication table. For 10 points, name these numbers expressible as "n times n," named for regular quadrilaterals.

perfect square numbers [do not accept or prompt on “perfect numbers”] (Paul Erdos’s proof for the more difficult portion of the theorem mentioned in the first line can be found in Proofs from the Book)

In this calendar decade, Alec Douglas-Home became the last Lord to be elected Prime Minister. In this decade, Enoch Powell advocated restricting immigration into Britain in the so-called "Rivers of Blood" speech. An affair with Christine Keeler led to the Profumo Affair in this decade. At the end of this decade, Edward Heath ended Harold Wilson's first ministry. (*) Harold Macmillan gave the "Wind of Change" speech at the start of this decade, and Britain gave independence to most of its African colonies in this decade. For 10 points, name this decade that was called "Swinging" for the popularity of "British invasion" bands like the Beatles.

In the Sonogashira coupling, terminal examples of these compounds can form carbon-carbon bonds after being deprotonated with bases. The Corey-Fuchs reaction forms these compounds from aldehydes. Sodium metal in ammonia or Lindlar catalyst, a poisoned catalyst, converts these compounds to alkenes. These compounds have carbon-hydrogen bonds with (*) sp hybridization. The simplest of these compounds is used in welding torches, has a C to H ratio of 1, has formula C2H2, and is called acetylene or ethyne. For 10 points, name these compounds characterized by a carbon-carbon triple bond, contrasted with alkanes and alkenes.
alkynes (“alk-ine” with a long i, like in the pronoun I) [do not accept or prompt on “alkane” or “alkene”]

This leader completed the restoration of the Etemenanki, a possible model for the Tower of Babel. This general defeated the army of Necho II at the Battle of Carchemish. This leader's father, along with Cyaxares of the Median Empire, sacked Nineveh to end the Assyrian Empire and was (*) Nabopolassar. This Chaldean leader defeated King Hezekiah to end the Kingdom of Judah and begin the Captivity. The mountain homeland of his wife Amytis supposedly led this leader to build the Hanging Gardens. For 10 points, name this builder of the Processional Way and the restored Ishtar Gate, the second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

Description acceptable. This object seems "as close as a star to the moon" to one character before its "colossal significance... vanished forever" and his "count of enchanted objects had diminished by one." In that man's first appearance, he "stretched out his arms... in a curious way" towards this object while "trembling." The narrator compares this object next to a "blue lawn" to "the (*) orgastic future that year by year recedes before us" and implies that trying to reach it would be like beating "boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past." For 10 points, name this object on Daisy Buchanan's dock, a symbol of unattainable status and love for Jay Gatsby.
The green light on Daisy Buchanan’s dock [or the green light from The Great Gatsby; prompt on light by asking “of what color?”]

This poem immediately succeeds a set of poems titled for "procreation" that encourage their subject to marry and bear children. This poem states that "every fair from fair sometime declines" but that "so long as men can breathe or eyes can see," it will "live and give life" to its subject. This poem describes the sun's varying warmth with the line "often is his gold complexion dimm'd." This poem's narrator laments the finitude of (*) "summer's lease" after noting that "Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May." For 10 points, name this poem by Shakespeare whose title question is answered, "Thou art more lovely and more temperate."
“Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” [accept Shakespeare’s Sonnet 18]

An author wrote a poem about translating this book that begins, "What is translation?" and calls translation "profanation of the dead"; collaborator Edmund Wilson later criticized the prose translation by that author, Vladimir Nabokov. A poetic stanza used in this book has the rhyme scheme ABABCCDDEFFEGG and a set pattern of masculine and feminine rhymes. It's not by (*) Turgenev, but this novel's title character is the trope of a cynical "superfluous man" used by later Russian authors. This novel's title character is a dandy ultimately rejected by his former lover Tatyana who kills Lensky in a senseless duel. For 10 points, name this verse novel by Alexander Pushkin.

This book warns against overvaluing "equality of condition" and excessive "individualism" that leads people to retreat into "little societies" while remaining "restless" about potentially losing their societies. This book's first part celebrates the township system and jury duty for promoting civic participation. This book suggests that in contrast with aristocracy, a "soft despotism" of conforming to custom and the despotism of the (*) "tyranny of the majority" may arise from its title institution. This book was inspired by an 1831 trip with Gustave de Beaumont to examine the American prison system. For 10 points, name this book by Alexis de Tocqueville analyzing democracy.
Democracy in America [or On Democracy in America; accept De La Démocratie en Amérique]

This author wrote about television's effect on fiction writers in "E Unibus Pluram." This author wrote that Roger Federer "re-embodied men's tennis" while comparing him to "religious experience." This author said that education's purpose was "learning how to be well-adjusted" in the boredom of adulthood in a commencement speech titled This Is Water. This author wrote about a Caribbean cruise trip in (*) "A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll Never Do Again" and debated the ethics of boiling animals alive in "Consider the Lobster." For 10 points, name this author of a novel where Quebecois radicals seek a film whose viewers die from repeatedly rewatching it, Infinite Jest.

In Reasons and Persons, Derek Parfit argued that optimizing either the total and average of this quantity in a population results in a contradiction and "repugnant conclusion." In Anarchy, State, and Utopia, Robert Nozick theorized a "monster" named for this quantity that gains more of it than anybody else does from the same scenario. This thinker names an effect where changes in price level affect spending through changes in interest rates. This thinker proposed a "liquidity trap" occurring when the LM line is horizontal. At the Bretton Woods Conference, this economist proposed the International Clearing Union, which became the IMF, based on proposals as a (*) delegate to the Treaty of Versailles that he wrote in The Economic Consequences of the Peace. Aggregate income and aggregate expenditure intersect at this economist's namesake "cross." For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who advocated deficit spending by the government in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.

This man kept his identity secret to his children with three German mistresses, calling himself "Careu Kent." This man and physician Alexis Carrel invented the perfusion pump, allowing organs to live outside the body before transplantation. Bruno Hauptmann supposedly used a ladder to kidnap a relative of this man from his room in the (*) "crime of the century." This man claimed that "Jewish groups" were pushing the US towards WWII while spokesperson for the America First Committee. For 10 points, name this man, most famous for a 33-hour action that began in Long Island and ended when he departed the Spirit of St Louis in Paris, the first transatlantic flight.

Note to players: The answer is a general category, such as "national parks," rather than a specific landform, like "waterfalls" A perspective for painting panoramic views of these places up to 150 degrees wide was developed by Paolo Panini. They're not ruins, but the term "capriccio" initially meant fantastical paintings combining scenes in these locations. The Stonemason's Yard is a scene of one of these places by a specialist in painting them. The rise of the Grand Tour resulted in more paintings of these locations in the vedute ("veh-DOO-tay") style by painters like (*) Canaletto, with smaller prints of them being used as postcard souvenirs by returning young men. For 10 points, paintings of St. Marks' Square and the Roman Forum showed scenes in what types of locations such as Venice and Rome?

The Guadiana River defines part of this country's western border, and the Guadalquivir River is the only major navigable river in it. A whistle language is used on this country's island of La Gomera to communicate long distances. This country's "Coast of Light" ends at its southernmost continental point, Tarifa. Palma is the capital of an archipelago in this country that contains Formentera and (*) Ibiza. This country's exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are on the coast of Morocco. This country's Andalusian city of Algeciras is the largest city on the Bay of Gibraltar. For 10 points, name this largest country on the Iberian Peninsula, with its capital at Madrid.

Moderator note: Read musical notes slowly. "Wer weiss, wie nahe mir mein Ende," transposes the first theme of this piece to "D, up to A, short G short F-sharp, G A B A," a theme from this piece's composer's opera Giustino ("jus-TEEN-oh"). This piece's third movement is an unusual 12/8 ("12 8") Allegro "danza pastorale" that imitates bagpipes while depicting "nymphs and shepherds lightly dancing" from an accompanying sonnet, while loud viola rhythms represent a (*) barking dog in its second movement. This piece is the first in The Contest Between Harmony and Invention. For 10 points, name this violin concerto famous for its musical depiction of birdsong, the first in Antonio Vivaldi's Four Seasons.

After an 1837 fire destroyed much of this building, its owner ordered that it be fully restored within a year. This Elizabethan Baroque building was the final work of architect Bartolomeo Rastrelli. This palace's throne room, St. George's Hall, was used for an inaugural 1906 parliamentary meeting. A 1920 reenactment at this palace killed more people than the initial event and inspired Ten Days That Shook the World, a documentary by (*) Sergei Eisenstein. This palace is the largest in the Hermitage Museum and was the royal palace during the fall of the Russian monarchy. For 10 points, name this St. Petersburg palace named for a season.

"Southern Country Mountains and Rivers," is often called this country's first declaration of independence. In this country, the luc bat ("luk BAHT") verse form was used for the epic The Tale of Kieu, written in its Chu Nom script. The Lover is an autobiographical novel about an affair with a Chinese man in this modern country, written by its native Marguerite Duras. An anonymous Communist spy narrates a Pulitzer-winning novel by an author born in this country, The (*) Sympathizer. An author born in this country created Little Dog, who writes letters to his mother in On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous. For 10 points, name this modern country where Ocean Vuong and Viet Thanh Nguyen ("win") were born.
Vietnam [or Socialist Republic of Vietnam or Cộng hòa xã hội chủ nghĩa Việt Nam]

In military slang, people who impersonate military heroes are called this character's name. This character is pestered to buy overshoes since he's "not a young man any longer." This character remembers the "what's-its-name" when he calls a district attorney a cur and is then laughed at for saying "puppy biscuit" out loud. This man hears multiple unrelated devices making similar (*) "pocketa-pocketa-pocketa" noises. While on a shopping trip for his wife, this man imagines himself as a sharpshooter, surgeon, and pilot. For 10 points, name this dreamy character created by James Thurber in a short story about his "secret life."

In this novel, a character returns from Cairo and is reminded of having said, "God bless you, God forgive you!" while standing in the "evening mists." The author retained the lines "I am greatly changed" and "suffering has been stronger than... teaching" after Wilkie Collins convinced him to rewrite its original "Piccadilly ending," where its protagonist is asked to speak to a lady in a carriage. This novel ends with the ambiguous litotes ("lye-TO-tees"), "I saw no shadow of another (*) parting from her," spoken at the ruins of Satis House, formerly Miss Havisham's house, where the protagonist reconnects with Estella. For 10 points, name this novel about Pip, by Charles Dickens.

John Hampden named this event while part of the ensuing Convention Parliament. This event was sparked by an "invitation" from the "Immortal Seven." This event's victor was soon embroiled in the broader Nine Years' War. The birth of the so-called "warming-pan baby" of Mary of Modena, James Francis Edward, sparked this event due to fears of a (*) Catholic king. This event saw its victor land an army at Brixham after issuing the Declaration of the Hague. This event resulted in the passage of a Bill of Rights and the reading of the Declaration of Right to the new monarchs, Mary II and William III. For 10 points, name this 1688 event that deposed King James II of England.

Note to moderator: Read letters of acrostic individually An undergraduate discovered that this poet encoded an acrostic "FFAALLAF," spelling "fall" in both directions, in a poem. A "brief epic" by this poet was inspired by a Thomas Ellwood question and was paired with a work whose last words are "all passion spent"; that closet drama's title character challenges Harapha despite being (*) "eyeless in Gaza." This author's most famous poem opens with an invocation to Urania and claims to "justify the ways of God to man." A character states that it is "better to reign in Hell, than to serve in Heaven" in that epic by this author. For 10 points, name this author of Samson Agonistes who dramatized the expulsion from Eden in Paradise Lost.

The first non-native Prince of Wales, who had this name, likely had a homosexual relationship with Piers Gaveston and features in a Chrisopher Marlowe play about his death at the hands of Roger and Isabella Mortimer; his successor as king with the same name executed the Mortimers. The British won the Battles of Poitiers under the (*) "Black Prince" of this name and Crecy under the third king of this name at the start of the Hundred Years' War. For 10 points, the Battle of Bannockburn was lost by the second king of what name, whose father of the same name had invaded Scotland and conquered Wales and was nicknamed "Longshanks"?

One man of this name was the first undisputed Habsburg Holy Roman Emperor. Another Holy Roman Emperor of this name wrote the earliest book on falconry, ruled during the Mongol invasion of Europe, and led a multicultural court from Palermo, Sicily that led him to be called "stupor mundi." That king was buried in the Kyffhauser mountains and will rise in Germany's time of need, a legend transferred to his grandfather of the same name who lost the Battle of (*) Legnano to the Lombard League. That Hohenstaufen emperor of this name died while crossing the Saleph River in the Third Crusade. For 10 points, what is the given name of Holy Roman Emperor "Barbarossa"?

This element's oxide was mined from the Ore Mountains to stain glass yellow, allowing it to be the first element discovered by Martin Klaproth. Two isotopes of this element with atomic mass differing by 4 are used to date samples between 100,000 and 1 million years old. Decreasing levels of this element in zircon crystals were used to show earth's age, as an isotope of this element has the (*) longest known half-life. A sample of this element that fogged a photographic plate allowed Henri Becquerel to discover radioactivity. This element's ore, pitchblende, was the source for the polonium and radium discovered by Marie Curie. For 10 points, name this heaviest natural element.

J. S. Bach's six trio sonatas for this instrument are among its hardest repertoire. Baroque terms denoting concert pitch and transposition an octave down, 8 and 16 foot pitch, are terms borrowed from this instrument. "Great" and "Swell" name the two most common manuals of this instrument. A virtuoso of this instrument walked 250 miles each way to hear Dietrich Buxtehude play it; that virtuoso was (*) Bach himself. The term "pedal point" originates from the loudest part of this instrument and features in the Toccata and Fugue in D minor written for it. For 10 points, name this large keyboard instrument that uses stops used to close off sets of pipes, often found in churches.

This scientist was the first to show that auroras were magnetic and names the sunspot minimum from 1790 to 1820. This scientist had colorblindness and was the first to describe it, so it is sometimes named for him. This scientist sometimes names the Law of Multiple Proportions, that masses of an element that react completely with a fixed mass of another element form simple ratios with each other. This scientist was the first to make a table of (*) atomic weights, so the atomic mass unit is named for him. This scientist names the law stating that in a gas mixture, partial pressures add. For 10 points, name this British chemist who introduced atomic theory into chemistry.

The western ends of the Raton Pass and Palo Flechado Pass lie in this state. This state's Mescalero Ridge is the western escarpment of the Staked Plains, a large mesa. This state's tallest mountain, Wheeler Peak, is in the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains, which end at this state's Glorieta Pass. The Pecos River originates in this state and flows through its city of (*) Roswell. An art colony in this state is located at Taos, the northernmost of its pueblos. The Rio Grande Gorge lies in this state, and the river forms the border between this state and Texas at El Paso. For 10 points, name this Southwestern state whose cities include Albuquerque and Santa Fe.

Thomas Carlyle described this god in "The Hero as Divinity" in his lectures outlining Great Man theory. Thor Heyerdahl's last project aimed to find evidence for this god's migration. A symbol of three interlocking triangles, the valknut, is thought to either be Hrungnir's heart or symbolize this god's ability to bind and unbind minds. This god found the (*) runes while hanging from Yggdrasil for nine days and nights, so he is accompanied by a horse with rune-incised teeth, Sleipnir. The earliest depictions of this warrior god are identifiable by the presence of Hugin and Munin, his ravens. For 10 points, name this one-eyed leader of the Aesir, the wisest Norse god.

In this work, the traveler Iagoo bears news of "warriors" from afar, one of whom is later welcomed as "the Black-Robe chief." Jane Johnston and Henry Rowe Schoolcraft's writings inspired this work. This work is in trochaic tetrameter and ends with its hero boating away westward with the arrival of Christianity, characteristics shared with the Kalevala. This poem's title character is (*) mistakenly named for the speaker of the Great Peacemaker. This epic poem occurs "by the shore of Gitche Gumee" and is loosely based upon Ojibwe myths of Manabozho's love for Minnehaha. For 10 points, name this "song" by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.

Cryptodires and pleurodires differ by the plane in which this structure is compressed. This structure's components include the atlas and axis. Zygapophyses help align the components of this structure. The branchial arches attach to this structure. Early 21st-century research showed that the simplest extant organisms to have this structure are hagfish. The (*) sacrum and coccyx are fused portions of this structure. Lancelets and tunicates lack this structure but still have a notochord, while the rest of phylum Chordata has both. For 10 points, name this structure that defines vertebrates, also called the backbone.
spine [accept backbone before mention; accept neck until “branchial”; accept vertebral column or spinal column; prompt on vertebrae; do not accept or prompt on “spinal cord”]

This writer argued that the Civil War was America's "only 'felt' history" in The Legacy of the Civil War. This writer interviewed civil rights activists in Who Speaks for the Negro? This writer repudiated his earlier segregationist essay "The Briar Patch" in I'll Take My Stand, a Southern Agrarian collection. This writer, who wrote Understanding Fiction with Cleanth Brooks, won Pulitzers in poetry for Promises and Now and Then and in (*) fiction for a novel in which human actions are ascribed to an impulsive "Great Twitch" by Jack Bundren. The Huey Long-inspired rise of gubernatorial candidate Willie Stark features in, for 10 points, what author's All the King's Men?

The Goetzes adapted a novel by this author into the film The Heiress. That novel ends with a character continuing fancywork "for life, as it were" after, at the persuasion of Mrs. Penniman, her fiance Morris Townsend abandons her despite her defying her father, Dr. Sloper. This author's possibly-lesbian character Olive Chancellor asks Verena Terrant not to marry, but she instead elopes with (*) ex-Confederate Basil Ransom and ends her feminist career. This author's New York Edition includes a novel in which Isabel Archer "affront[s] her destiny." For 10 points, name this author of Washington Square, The Bostonians, and The Portrait of a Lady.

Michel Brunet's ("mee-SHEL BRU-nay's") team discovered the oldest known hominins in this country's Djourab Depression. Diatom remains from a dried lakebed in this country's Bodele Depression forms dust that fertilizes the Amazon Rainforest. This country's president Goukouni Oueddei ("goo-KOO-nee weh-DAY") was one of its Toubou ("too-boo") people, who live near its highest point of Emi Koussi in the Tibesti Mountains. The Chari River flows into this country's largest lake, which has (*) shrunk 90% since the 1960s. This country defended the Aouzou Strip in a war with Libya to its north. For 10 points, name this country that names the largest lake in West Africa and has its capital at N'Djamena.

This author criticizes elevating the rationality of man, a "miserable and wretched creature," instead advocating skepticism by asking, "What do I know?" John Florio's translation of this author inspired Gonzalo's speech about a "commonwealth" where "All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour" in The Tempest. This author's encounter with Tupinamba from the (*) New World led him to compare Europeans "tearing a body limb from limb" negatively to their custom "to roast and eat him after he is dead" in "Of Cannibals." For 10 points, name this French author who popularized a new genre of "attempts" in Essays.

Note to moderator: Read mathematical expressions slowly This scientist invented and named the solenoid. This scientist's "force law" contains the term "dl sub 1 cross the quantity dl sub 2 cross r hat" to combine the Biot-Savart Law with the equation for magnetic force. A term of "1 over c squared dE/dt" was added to a law named for this scientist to account for a "displacement current." This scientist's "circuit law" states that the (*) line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop equals the permeability of free space times enclosed current; that law is one of Maxwell's Equations along with Gauss's Law and Faraday's Law. For 10 points, name this Frenchman, the namesake of the SI unit for current.

Friedrich Wilhelm Gustav Bruhn invented a device for these vehicles, which Frederick Greiner included in the first gas-powered one, the Daimler Victoria. One type of these vehicles was invented by Joseph Hansom and had a lower center of gravity than earlier hackney carriages. These vehicles were commandeered by Joseph Gallieni to transfer soldiers to the First Battle of the Marne. Certain drivers of these vehicles had larger (*) hippocampuses than typical since to obtain their medallion licenses, they needed to have comprehensive memories of London streets. For 10 points, name these vehicles that can be hailed for rides and are often painted yellow.
taxicabs [accept cabs; prompt on cars or carriages; accept answers including Stuttgart, London or Paris]

Juan Perez was the first European to reach this modern administrative region, where he traded with Chief Maquinna of the Nuu-chah-nulth. Jose Martinez declared Spanish sovereignty in this modern administrative region despite John Meares's presence, causing the Nootka Crisis. James Cook's final voyage connected partial maps of this region made by voyages from neighboring Russian and (*) Spanish territories. Trade in otter pelts prompted border disputes in this province containing the northern half of Oregon Country. This province's southern border was thought to be the Northwest Passage by Juan de Fuca. George Vancouver names, for 10 points, the largest island and city of what Canadian province?

British Columbia [or BC; prompt on Oregon Country or Oregon Territory by asking “what modern administrative region”; prompt on Pacific Northwest; antiprompt on Vancouver Island by asking “what modern administrative region is that in”]

Note to players: Please give an answer in English This topic is the subject of the work Lysis. Aristophanes explains this concept by saying that humans used to be cartwheeling spheres who were split when they attacked Olympus. After its title character repeats a bad speech by Lysias on this topic, Socrates makes two speeches on it, the latter including the chariot allegory-where a bad horse is tamed by this concept-in Phaedrus. After arriving late drunk, Alcibiades states that he follows Socrates due to this (*) feeling. This concept is a daemon according to Diotima and helps people follow the "form of beauty," leading them to seek knowledge. For 10 points, name this subject of Plato's Symposium, where men give speeches in praise of the god Eros.
love [accept friendship; prompt on beauty by asking “what feeling does the viewer of beauty have?”]

Yawarkucha, a lake in this country, was named for being filled with the blood of a defeated Caranqui rebellion. This country's Las Vegas culture preceded a culture that Betty Meggers falsely claimed had contact with the Jomon, the Valdivia culture. This country was the primary source of Strombus and Spondylus shells and balsa rafts. This country's Canari city of Tomebamba was likely meant to become a second capital for (*) Huayna Capac after his campaigns in this country. Atahualpa's mother was from this country, and he won the Incan Civil War with the allegiance of the northern Incan army here. For 10 points, name this country home to the Kingdom of Quito.

Neutron activation analysis to find this material's trace element composition informs scholars on long-distance trade routes from its rare sources. The ability of this material to pick up air moisture allows its "hydration" to be used to date when it was last flaked. This material easily forms conchoidal fractures when struck, allowing it to be made into the best prismatic blades or (*) projectile points, sharper than steel. This material was polished to make "smoking mirrors" prized in Mesoamerica. For 10 points, name this igneous rock, a dark-colored volcanic glass.
obsidian [prompt on volcanic glass; do not accept or prompt on “glass”]

The Bruun Rule describes profiles of these places. Strand plains in these places have troughs called swales between them, while elevated berms form in the back of them. Groins in these places stop a physical "refraction" generated by oblique wind causing the two halves of swash having different angles. These places can be green from olivine, like at Papakolea, or black from volcanic rock, like at Punaluu. These places are subject to (*) longshore drift. Dunes form inland of these places, while these places are immediately inland of the breaker zone, or surf zone. For 10 points, name these places whose terrain consists of small particles along a coast, where tourists often go to collect seashells.

According to Vergil, this figure could not finish carving the doors of the Temple of Apollo at Cumae out of grief. Athena turned this figure's nephew into a partridge after this figure jealously threw him off the Acropolis. In some accounts, this figure killed a pursuer by pouring boiling water into his bath after being discovered from using honey and an ant to (*) thread a seashell. This figure made a wooden cow to help Pasiphae mate with a bull and imprisoned the offspring within a labyrinth on the orders of King Minos. For 10 points, name this craftsman who escaped Crete on waxen wings but whose son, Icarus, died when his wings melted from flying too close to the son.

Moderator note: Read musical notes slowly. One theme in this work begins "G long G, C G, up to E E long F E" and is played by a screeching E-flat clarinet in its last movement; earlier, it is truncated by a tutti G minor chord and descending bass pizzicato. In this work's last movement, bells accompany a low entry of the ophicleides and bassoons beginning "E-flat D E-flat C D." This work's third movement features a cor anglais and offstage oboe in a (*) "Scene in the country." This work, an "Episode in the Life of an Artist in Five Movements," features the Dies Irae in a "Dream of a Witches' Sabbath" following a "March to the Scaffold." The idee fixe is central to, for 10 points, what symphony about an opium-induced dream by Hector Berlioz?
Symphonie Fantastique: Épisode de la vie d’un artiste … en cinq parties

This leader's second wife Scribonia voluntarily joined their daughter exiled for adultery at Pandateria. That daughter had been married to this leader's closest male relative, Marcus Claudius Marcellus, before his early death. This leader supposedly died from poisoned figs given by his wife, although some suggest that he purposely timed his death to prevent the succession of (*) Agrippa Postumus, the youngest son of his daughter Julia the Elder. This leader's final wife had previously married Tiberius Claudius Nero, thus making his successor a member of the Claudian family. For 10 points, name this Roman emperor succeeded by Tiberius, the first emperor of Rome.

These devices' quality can be measured by the size of the "circle of least confusion." The terms "coma" and "spherical aberration" refer to distortions created by these devices. The difference between the reciprocals of two radii of curvature is proportional to their strength in an equation named for "makers" of these devices. The sum of the reciprocals of object distance and image distance equals the reciprocal of the (*) focal length of these devices in an equation named for their "thin" type, and the negative image length over the object length equals their magnification. For 10 points, name these devices that, unlike mirrors, bend and focus light and are found in cameras and eyeglasses.

This thinker defined secondary substances as universals and primary substances as individuals' essences in the theory of hylomorphism. This thinker described an active intellect that is "deathless and everlasting" and required for all thinking in On the Soul. This thinker characterized all things into four kinds and ten categories. This thinker described material, formal, efficient, and final as the four types of (*) causes, the last of which God is, acting through love as the "unmoved mover" in this thinker's Metaphysics. This thinker claimed eudaimonia, or happiness, as the good in Nicomachean Ethics. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher, a student of Plato.

Amphibolite forms from metamorphism of rocks with minerals high in these two metallic elements, such as hornblende. Olivine and pyroxene make up peridotite, a rock classified as "ultra" rich in these two elements and a major component of the mantle. "Intermediate" rocks such as gabbro and basalt have compositions between rocks with more of these two elements and rocks with more potassium and aluminum, which are also more siliceous. These two elements distinguish (*) igneous rocks with higher density and darker color, which are called "mafic" due to these elements' Latin names. For 10 points, name these two elements with chemical symbols Mg and Fe.

This character's author stated that his most ingenious actions occur before being attacked by the Cunninghams in Reigate. Under the name Altamont, this character opens a safe with the combination "August 1914," owned by the German agent Von Bork. "Fred Porlock" sends this character a warning about a Mr. Douglas at Birlstone, who had posed as Jack McMurdo to defeat the Scowrers and was actually (*) Birdy Edwards. This character captures the vengeful lover of Lucy Ferrier, who was forced into a Mormon marriage despite her love for the cab driver Jefferson Hope, in A Study in Scarlet. For 10 points, name this detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle who collaborates with Dr. Watson.

In the microcanonical ensemble, this quantity for each microstate equals 1 over the number of microstates by the first postulate of statistical mechanics, which states that microstates with equal N, V, and E have equal values for it. This quantity for a particle is proportional to the square of its wave function. Orbitals are drawn to show regions where the "cumulative density" of this quantity is above (*) 0.95 or 0.9. Wave-particle duality and the uncertainty principle mean that electron locations can only be referred to by the value of this quantity that they have in a given region. For 10 points, name this unitless quantity that denotes how likely an event occurs.

Moderator note: Read musical notes slowly. Composer and type of piece required. One of these pieces in C minor was published with a "Fantasy" in the same key and begins with a Mannheim rocket in octaves. The "Durnitz" is the last of the "Munich" ones of these pieces, the first six by their composer. Max Reger wrote "variations and a fugue" on the theme of an A major Andante grazioso movement in one of these works. "Long C, E G long low B, C D, C" accompanied by an (*) Alberti bass begins the "Facile" ("FA-chee-lay") one of these works. A "B A G-sharp A C" motif begins the last movement of one of these pieces, which is in arch form despite being nicknamed "Rondo alla Turca." For 10 points, name these three-movement works for solo piano by Mozart.
piano sonatas by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart [prompt on partial answer] (The first line is about Piano Sonata No. 14)

This quantity can be expressed as "-2 times mass, times omega cross dr/dt." The ratio of inertial forces to this quantity is the Rossby number. This force's namesake effect is similar to the Eotvos ("UT-vush") effect, caused by the centrifugal force. Foucault's Pendulum precesses due to this force. The Euler force, centrifugal force, and this force result when working in a (*) rotating reference frame. This fictitious force deflects objects in rotating reference frames to the side, which is the cause of prevailing winds on earth. For 10 points, name this force responsible for making cyclones rotate differently in different hemispheres, named for a Frenchman.

This figure twice speaks the phrase "for it is better for me to die than to live" to God. "The earth with her bars was about me forever" is part of a prayer by this figure that begins, "I called to the Lord out of my distress, and he answered me." This son of Amittai tells a king that his city will be destroyed in forty days and goes to the desert to watch its fate; there, God creates a (*) gourd to give him shade, then a worm to destroy the gourd, and chides him for being angry at the gourd's destruction and city's salvation. This person is thrown overboard in a storm he caused by disobeying God's orders to preach to Nineveh. For 10 points, name this prophet swallowed by a whale.

Whitney Houston and Mariah Carey made a recording of this studio's first Academy Award-winning song, "When You Believe." One of this studio's characters probably lampoons Michael Eisner due to his animosity with one of its founders, Jeffrey Katzenberg. After Sinbad: Legend of the Seven Seas nearly bankrupted it, this studio became one of the first of its kind to go fully digital in production. This studio likely criticized Disney with a Pinocchio-inspired (*) bug admonishing a villain hoarding fairy tale objects, Jack Horner. This studio's subversions of fairy tales include an antagonist Prince Charming for ogre protagonists. For 10 points, name this animation studio of The Prince of Egypt and Shrek.
DreamWorks Animation [accept DreamWorks Pictures, even though that’s the live action studio]

This figure's horse is called "bad weather today" in one country after a man playing his assistant on TV misheard a question, while it is named Oznosel in another country after Amerigo retired. Jan ("yahn") Schenkman popularized a tradition of this figure living in a Spanish castle and steamboating into port in mid-November. Soot now often replaces blackface in the makeup for this figure's Moorish helper, who traditionally had a birch rod for spanking and is (*) "Black Pete." In Belgium and the Netherlands, this figure's feast on December 6th is an occasion for giving children gifts. For 10 points, name this patron saint of children, syncretized in the English-speaking world with Father Christmas.

Sinterklaas [or Saint Nicholas or Sint-Nicolaas; generously prompt on Santa Claus by asking “traditions around which saint are the source of some traditions around Santa?”; prompt on De Goede Sint or The Good Saint or De Goedheiligman by asking “which saint?”; do not accept or prompt on “Father Christmas”]

This country's anthropologist Teuku Jacob controversially damaged specimens found there while trying to show that they were Homo sapiens. Eugene Dubois discovered a skull in this country in 1891, the first to be called the "pithecanthropus," on its Solo River; that skull is now the type specimen of Homo erectus. A species of hominin only found in this country was discovered in Liang Bua Cave in 2003; that species is thought to have survived until (*) modern humans arrived 50,000 years ago and had an adult height of under four feet. For 10 points, name this Asian country home to Homo floresiensis, also called the "Hobbit," and the specimen "Java Man."

These people believe that Eli usurped the high priesthood and made the altar at Shiloh with a fake Ark of the Covenant. Most of these people live near the site of Moses's first blessings in Canaan, which they also consider the site of the Sacrifice of Isaac and Noah's Ark, Mount Gerizim. These people consider a Torah written in their own Semitic language the only true scripture. Although these people were hated by the Jews, in response to the question, "Who is my neighbor?," one of them was contrasted with a (*) priest and a Levite for helping a man robbed on the road to Jericho. For 10 points, a "Good" one of what people is the subject of a parable of Jesus on helping those in need?

The roadless Mahale Mountains National Park is east of this lake, and it is the largest lake directly east of the Mitumba Mountains. The Malagarasi River forms a national border before ending in this lake. The Ruzizi River drains Lake Kivu into this lake. This lake was the largest reached by Burton and Speke; Burton then falsely claimed it as the source of the Nile. This lake is the largest in the Albertine Rift, and it drains via the Lukuga into the (*) Lualaba River. Among freshwater lakes, this lake is the second oldest, second deepest, and longest. For 10 points, name this African Great Lake that used to name non-Zanzibar Tanzania and drains into the Congo River system.

Butterfly McQueen made her film debut as Prissy in this film. Kay Brown Barrett first suggested this film's plot to its producer and consulted with Walter White of the NAACP on its black characters. Description or specific answer acceptable. Ditungsten gas has the highest known value for this quantity, a mark previously held by bonded chromium atoms with terphenyl ligands. Moderator note: Read the mathematical expression slowly The AKS primality test was the first that could generally and deterministically run in this time complexity without relying on conjectures. This particle's root mean square charge radius was found to be around 0.833 femtometers in 2019. After "capturing" an electron, these particles become (*) neutrally-charged and a high-velocity neutrino is emitted. These particles decay into an antimuon and neutral pion in at least 6.6 times 10 to the 33rd years, though this process has never been observed. For 10 points, name these positively-charged particles composed of two up quarks and one down quark.

One side of this battle made use of Sherden mercenaries, which were folded into their general's personal guard. One record of this battle was found at Bogazkoy, and two Shasu nomads pretended to be deserters and gave one side false information before it. One side of this battle was split into divisions such as the (*) Ptah and Amun, and it was fought along the Orontes River. Fifteen years after this battle's conclusion, its two generals signed the oldest surviving peace treaty. For 10 points, name this inconclusive battle fought between Muwatalli II's Hittites and Ramses II's Egyptians, the largest chariot battle in history.

Charles Villiers motioned for the repeal of this legislation for eight consecutive years. Richard Cobden founded a "league" advocating for the repeal of these laws, and James Wilson created The Economist to build support for their repeal. These laws were introduced during the Premiership of Lord Liverpool, and were supported by economist Thomas (*) Malthus. These laws were finally repealed during the Irish Potato Famine under Prime Minister Robert Peel. For 10 points, name these series of tariffs placed upon British grain.

A shoe made from several leather scraps is used in this event by a participant who resides in Idavoll at its conclusion. Hodmimer's holt is used as a hideout by Lif and her lover during this event and the three winters that precede it. A sword that shines "brighter than the sun" is used by Surt as he leads the sons of (*) Muspel in this event. Three roosters and the Gjallarhorn announce the start of this event. Jormungandr is killed during this event by Thor, who dies from poisoning after taking nine steps. For 10 points, name this event that encompasses the deaths of Loki and the Aesir as the ultimate battle in Norse mythology.

This building was third on the list of buildings featured in the PBS documentary series 10 Buildings that Changed America. The two architects that designed this building also collaborated on the Auditorium Building in Chicago. This building has a base-shaft-attic design, with its bottom two floors faced in brown sandstone and the higher floors including "honeycomb" offices. (*) Terra cotta is prominently displayed on this building, which is sometimes considered the first to successfully utilize steel frame construction. For 10 points, name this Adler and Sullivan construction named for a local brewer and financier in downtown St. Louis.
